corrected_value.authors: Sachdeva, S., Iliev, R., & Medin, D. L.
corrected_value.title: Sinning saints and saintly sinners: The paradox of moral self-regulation.

decisions.quote:
The present work includes three attempts to replicate the moral licensing effect by Sachdeva, Iliev, and Medin (2009). The original
    authors found that writing about positive traits led to lower donations to charity and decreased cooperative behavior. The first two replication
    attempts (student samples, 95% power based on the initial findings, NStudy1 = 105, NStudy2 = 150), did not confirm the original results. The third
    replication attempt (MTurk sample, 95% power based on a meta-analysis on self-licensing, N = 940) also did not confirm the moral licensing
    effect.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding (target 0) correctly identify Sachdeva, Iliev, and Medin (2009), 'Sinning saints and saintly sinners: The paradox of moral self-regulation', as the single tested original study. Replication Studies 1, 2, and 3 directly re-test Original Studies 1 and 3 (using Study 2's clarified recall instruction in Study 1).

decisions.quote:
The present work includes three attempts to replicate the moral licensing effect by Sachdeva, Iliev, and Medin (2009). The original
    authors found that writing about positive traits led to lower donations to charity and decreased cooperative behavior. The first two replication
    attempts (student samples, 95% power based on the initial findings, NStudy1 = 105, NStudy2 = 150), did not confirm the original results. The third
    replication attempt (MTurk sample, 95% power based on a meta-analysis on self-licensing, N = 940) also did not confirm the moral licensing
    effect. We conclude that (1) there is as of yet no strong support for the moral self-regulation framework proposed in Sachdeva et al. (2009) (2)
    the manipulation used is unlikely to induce moral licensing, and (3) studies on moral licensing should use a neutral control condition.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding agree on 'failed'. Across all three high-powered replication studies (N = 105, N = 150, N = 940), the central moral licensing effect on charitable donations and cooperative behavior failed to replicate, and the authors state an explicit overall verdict that none of the three attempts confirmed the moral licensing effect and that there is no strong support for the moral self-regulation framework proposed by Sachdeva et al. (2009) (with their meta-analyses across studies showing null effects for both moral licensing, p = .603, and moral cleansing, p = .593, despite a single moral cleansing comparison on donations in Study 3).
